mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly defines repolarisation in a nerve impulse and distinguishes it from depolarisation?

options.A: Repolarisation restores the membrane potential to negative values after depolarisation, mainly by K⁺ efflux, whereas depolarisation is the initial rise in potential caused by Na⁺ influx.
options.B: Repolarisation is the initial rise in membrane potential due to Na⁺ influx, while depolarisation maintains the resting potential.
options.C: Repolarisation involves opening of voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels that make the membrane more positive, opposite to depolarisation.
options.D: Repolarisation is caused by passive diffusion of Cl⁻ ions that hyperpolarise the membrane and is unrelated to depolarisation.

mcqs.answer: Repolarisation restores the membrane potential to negative values after depolarisation, mainly by K⁺ efflux, whereas depolarisation is the initial rise in potential caused by Na⁺ influx.
mcqs.explanation: During an action potential, depolarisation occurs when voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes into the cell, making the interior less negative. Repolarisation follows as those Na⁺ channels close and voltage‑gated K⁺ channels open, allowing K⁺ to leave the cell, bringing the membrane potential back toward its negative resting value. Options B, C and D describe incorrect mechanisms.

mcqs.question: A neuron has just completed an action potential. Which statement best describes what happens during the absolute refractory period?

options.A: Voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated, so no new action potential can be triggered regardless of stimulus strength.
options.B: Only a very strong stimulus can open Na⁺ channels, allowing a new action potential to start.
options.C: K⁺ channels remain closed, keeping the membrane permanently depolarised.
options.D: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump stops working, causing the membrane potential to stay at zero.

mcqs.answer: Voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated, so no new action potential can be triggered regardless of stimulus strength.
mcqs.explanation: In the absolute refractory period, the Na⁺ channels that opened during the previous spike are in an inactivated state; they cannot reopen until the membrane returns to near‑resting potential. Therefore, no amount of stimulus can elicit another action potential. Option B describes the relative refractory period, while C and D are inaccurate descriptions of neuronal physiology.

mcqs.question: Which of the following examples correctly illustrates saltatory conduction of an action potential?

options.A: An action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next along a myelinated axon, greatly increasing conduction speed.
options.B: An action potential propagates continuously along an unmyelinated axon, with the wave of depolarisation moving smoothly.
options.C: A muscle fiber contracts uniformly because calcium ions diffuse rapidly throughout the cytoplasm.
options.D: A sensory receptor generates a graded potential that spreads passively without any active propagation.

mcqs.answer: An action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next along a myelinated axon, greatly increasing conduction speed.
mcqs.explanation: Saltatory conduction occurs only in myelinated axons where the myelin sheath forces the depolarising current to flow to the exposed nodes of Ranvier. The action potential appears to ‘jump’ between nodes, making transmission faster than the continuous wave seen in unmyelinated fibers (option B). Options C and D describe unrelated processes.

mcqs.question: A neuron at rest has a high concentration of K⁺ inside the cell and a high concentration of Na⁺ outside. Which ion movement contributes most directly to the establishment of the resting membrane potential?

options.A: Passive diffusion of K⁺ out of the cell through leak channels.
options.B: Active transport of Na⁺ into the cell by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.
options.C: Opening of voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels causing Na⁺ influx.
options.D: Efflux of Cl⁻ ions through chloride channels.

mcqs.answer: Passive diffusion of K⁺ out of the cell through leak channels.
mcqs.explanation: At rest, the membrane is most permeable to K⁺, which leaks out through open K⁺ channels, leaving behind negatively charged proteins and establishing a negative interior (~‑70 mV). The Na⁺/K⁺ pump (option B) maintains the gradients but contributes only a small electrogenic effect. Voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels (C) are closed at rest, and Cl⁻ movement (D) has a minor role.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements about depolarisation is a common misconception?

options.A: Depolarisation occurs because voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels open, allowing Na⁺ to flow into the cell.
options.B: Depolarisation is the phase when the membrane potential becomes less negative than the resting potential.
options.C: Depolarisation happens when K⁺ channels open and K⁺ leaves the cell, making the interior more positive.
options.D: Depolarisation is initiated by a stimulus that reaches the threshold, triggering Na⁺ influx.

mcqs.answer: Depolarisation happens when K⁺ channels open and K⁺ leaves the cell, making the interior more positive.
mcqs.explanation: The correct mechanism for depolarisation is the opening of voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels, not K⁺ channels. When K⁺ leaves the cell (option C), the interior actually becomes more negative, which is part of repolarisation. Options A, B, and D accurately describe depolarisation.

mcqs.question: If voltage‑gated Na⁺ channels close earlier than usual during an action potential, what is the most likely effect on the repolarisation phase?

options.A: Repolarisation will begin sooner and may be completed more rapidly.
options.B: Repolarisation will be delayed because Na⁺ influx continues longer.
options.C: The amplitude of the action potential will increase, but repolarisation timing remains unchanged.
options.D: There will be no effect on repolarisation because it depends only on K⁺ channel activity.

mcqs.answer: Repolarisation will begin sooner and may be completed more rapidly.
mcqs.explanation: Repolarisation is triggered when Na⁺ channels close and K⁺ channels open. If Na⁺ channels close earlier, the inward positive current stops sooner, allowing the outward K⁺ current to dominate earlier, thus initiating repolarisation sooner. Option B is opposite, C is unrelated, and D ignores the role of Na⁺ channel closure.

mcqs.question: Which pair of statements correctly compares the absolute and relative refractory periods?

options.A: During the absolute refractory period no stimulus can elicit an action potential, whereas during the relative refractory period a stronger-than‑normal stimulus can.
options.B: Both periods allow any stimulus to generate a new action potential, but the relative period lasts longer.
options.C: The absolute refractory period occurs after repolarisation, while the relative refractory period occurs before depolarisation.
options.D: During the absolute refractory period Na⁺ channels are open, whereas during the relative period they are closed.

mcqs.answer: During the absolute refractory period no stimulus can elicit an action potential, whereas during the relative refractory period a stronger-than‑normal stimulus can.
mcqs.explanation: In the absolute refractory period, Na⁺ channels are inactivated, making a new action potential impossible regardless of stimulus strength. In the subsequent relative refractory period, some Na⁺ channels have recovered, so a suprathreshold stimulus can trigger another spike. Options B, C, and D misrepresent the timing and channel states.

mcqs.question: All of the following are true about saltatory conduction in myelinated axons EXCEPT:

options.A: It increases the speed of nerve impulse transmission compared with unmyelinated fibers.
options.B: Action potentials are regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier.
options.C: Myelin sheath allows continuous flow of ions along the entire length of the axon.
options.D: The myelin sheath reduces the capacitance of the axonal membrane.

mcqs.answer: Myelin sheath allows continuous flow of ions along the entire length of the axon.
mcqs.explanation: Myelin insulates the axon, preventing ion flow across the membrane except at the nodes of Ranvier; thus ion movement is not continuous along the whole axon (option C is false). Options A, B, and D correctly describe the increased speed, regeneration at nodes, and reduced membrane capacitance due to myelin.
